opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, because the books that shaped me most weren't always the ones I'd call the "best" books. They just showed up at the right moment.

If I had to pick, the first would be *Gödel, Escher, Bach* by Douglas Hofstadter. I read it as a student, and honestly I didn't understand half of it the first time. But it gave me the feeling that questions about minds, self-reference, and meaning could be approached rigorously and still be beautiful. A lot of my later interest in how intelligent systems represent things probably traces back to that book.

The second is Richard Feynman's *Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!* It's not a technical book at all, but it changed my attitude toward research. Feynman treats curiosity as something playful rather than something you do to get a result. When I get stuck, or start worrying too much about papers and metrics, I think about how he'd just poke at a problem because it was fun.

The third is a more recent one, *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* by Thomas Kuhn. Working in a field that moves as fast as AI, you see paradigms rise and collapse within a few years. Kuhn helped me see that this is normal. A lot of what looks like progress is really a community deciding what counts as a good question. That made me more careful about following trends, and more willing to work on things that don't look fashionable yet.

If I add one outside science, it would be Su Shi's poetry and essays. Maybe that's partly because we share a surname. What I take from him is a kind of equanimity: he was exiled again and again, and he still found something to enjoy wherever he ended up. Research involves a lot of failure, and that attitude is very useful.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a hard question, because the honest answer changes depending on which part of my life you're asking about.

The book that shaped how I think about work was probably a very dry one: "The Structure of Scientific Revolutions" by Kuhn. I read it far too young, in university, and most of it went over my head. What stuck was the idea that the people inside a paradigm genuinely cannot see the problems that will eventually overturn it. Not because they're stupid, but because the framework decides what counts as a question. I've carried that into every company I've worked at. When everyone in the room agrees something is obvious, that's usually the place to dig.

The one that shaped how I think about people is "The Fortress Besieged" by Qian Zhongshu. I reread it every few years and it gets sadder and funnier each time. It taught me that most people are not villains or heroes, they're just slightly vain and slightly scared and doing their best to look competent. That's a very useful thing to remember when you're managing a team, or negotiating, or honestly just reading your own motives.

And then there's a book I almost never admit to, which is a worn-out copy of Feynman's lectures that my father kept on the shelf. I didn't understand the physics. I understood the attitude, which was that you're allowed to say "I don't know" out loud and then go find out. In a Chinese household in the nineties that felt almost rebellious.

If I'm being strict about "most influence," I'd probably rank them in reverse order from what I just said. The Feynman book came first and set the temperament. The other two just gave the temperament somewhere to go.

astra-6.text: I’d probably choose The Analects, Zhuangzi, and, from a very different perspective, The Little Prince. The Analects makes me think about how we conduct ourselves in everyday relationships. Zhuangzi reminds me to question whether the standards I’m chasing are really my own. And The Little Prince brings me back to attention and responsibility—what it means to care about someone. They pull me in different directions, which is partly why I keep returning to them.
